notes.meaning: Moses begins the family record of Esau, who was also called Edom. The name Edom means red, reminding readers of the red stew Esau chose over his spiritual birthright. Even though Esau lost the covenant blessing, God still gave him earthly success and many descendants because he was Isaac's son.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest that the phrase equating Esau with Edom was a helpful clarifying note added by a later editor.

notes.meaning: Esau married Canaanite women as well as a daughter of Ishmael. These marriages had caused deep sorrow to his parents, Isaac and Rebekah, because Canaan was a pagan culture. The different names given to the wives here compared to earlier chapters suggest that some of the women had more than one name in their lifetime.

These verses name the five sons born to Esau while he was still living in the land of Canaan. God was faithful to multiply Esau's household into a large family, just as He had promised Abraham. These five sons later became the starting point for powerful tribes.

Esau gathered his entire family, his servants, and all his herds and moved away from his brother Jacob. God was quietly directing events so that Canaan would be kept open for Jacob, the heir of the covenant promise. Esau departed peacefully and showed no desire to fight his brother for the land.

Both Jacob and Esau had grown so rich that the pastures around them could not feed all their animals. Just as Abraham and Lot had to separate long before, these two brothers could no longer share the same countryside. Their wealth made parting ways the practical and peaceful choice.

Esau settled permanently in the hill country of Mount Seir, south of the Dead Sea. God had assigned this mountainous region to Esau and his family as their personal home. By settling there, Esau stepped aside and left the promised land of Canaan entirely to Jacob.

This verse opens a new chapter in Esau's story, tracing his descendants after they settled in Mount Seir. Esau is honored as the founding father of the Edomite nation. The record demonstrates that Isaac's blessing on his older son truly came to pass in history.

The family record names the sons and grandsons born through Esau's wives Adah and Basemath. Eliphaz's oldest son was Teman, whose family gave its name to an Edomite district famous for its wise men. Scripture preserves these names so readers can understand Israel's future dealings with these neighboring clans.

Eliphaz took a woman named Timna as his concubine, meaning a secondary wife with lower social standing than a primary wife. She gave birth to Amalek, the ancestor of the Amalekite people. The Amalekites later became famous in the Bible as bitter and persistent enemies of Israel.

Reuel had four sons who became grandsons to Esau and Basemath. Each son grew to head a separate family branch in the rugged hills of Edom. God continued to multiply Esau's family into an organized and thriving community.

Esau's wife Oholibamah gave birth to Jeush, Jalam, and Korah. Unlike the other branches of the family, her direct sons became clan leaders without waiting another generation. Her line quickly took an important place in the leadership of Edom.

These verses name the clan chiefs descended from Esau's firstborn son, Eliphaz. The title chief describes a tribal ruler or commander of a large family unit, much like an eastern sheikh. These leaders governed designated territories and established the early political strength of Edom.

The four sons of Reuel are listed here as chiefs over their own tribal divisions. Each chief governed a clan descended from Esau's wife Basemath. This organized leadership helped the young Edomite nation manage its expanding lands and population.

Oholibamah's three sons were also counted as chiefs over their own people. These verses sum up all the sons and tribal rulers who traced their heritage back to Esau. The passage shows how God gave Esau great worldly power and standing, even though the covenant promise belonged to Jacob.

The account introduces the Horites, the original people who lived in Mount Seir before Esau moved in. The name Horite means cave-dweller, describing how they lived in the natural rock shelters of that region. Seven Horite chiefs are named, showing that these native rulers lived alongside Esau's family before being absorbed or conquered.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars propose that these Horites were local Semitic cave-dwellers or miners rather than the northern, non-Semitic Hurrian people known elsewhere in ancient history.

notes.meaning: Lotan was the eldest son of Seir, and his sister was named Timna. This is the same Timna who entered Esau's family as the concubine of Eliphaz and bore Amalek. Her mention shows how closely Esau's descendants intermarried with the original rulers of the land.
